summary: The note is the Wikipedia article on the likelihood-ratio test, a statistical method that compares the goodness of fit of two competing models by the ratio of their likelihoods, with a constrained model (the null hypothesis) against an unconstrained one. It explains the test statistic λLR = −2 ln(sup over Θ0 of L / sup over Θ of L), notes that the test is also called Wilks test and is the oldest of the three classical tests alongside the Lagrange multiplier and Wald tests, and covers the simple-hypothesis case justified by the Neyman–Pearson lemma. It also gives a worked normal-mean example yielding a t-statistic relation and states Wilks' theorem, under which the statistic is asymptotically chi-squared with degrees of freedom equal to the difference in dimensionality of the parameter spaces.
one_line: Wikipedia article on the likelihood-ratio test, a statistical method comparing goodness of fit of nested models via their likelihood ratio, asymptotically chi-squared under Wilks' theorem.
key_facts: The likelihood-ratio test assesses the goodness of fit of two competing statistical models, one found by maximization over the entire parameter space and another found after imposing a constraint.
The likelihood-ratio test is also known as Wilks test and is the oldest of the three classical approaches to hypothesis testing, together with the Lagrange multiplier test and the Wald test.
The likelihood ratio test statistic is λLR = −2 ln[sup over θ in Θ0 of L(θ) / sup over θ in Θ of L(θ)].
As all likelihoods are positive and the constrained maximum cannot exceed the unconstrained maximum, the likelihood ratio is bounded between zero and one.
The Neyman–Pearson lemma justifies the likelihood-ratio test for comparing two models with no unknown parameters and shows the test has the highest power among all competitors.
The likelihood-ratio test requires that the models be nested, meaning the more complex model can be transformed into the simpler model by imposing constraints on its parameters.

Under Wilks' theorem, assuming the null hypothesis is true, λLR converges asymptotically to a chi-squared distribution as sample size approaches infinity, if the null lies strictly within the interior of the parameter space.
The chi-squared degrees of freedom equal the difference in dimensionality of the parameter spaces Θ and Θ0.
The finite-sample distributions of likelihood-ratio statistics are generally unknown.
Many common test statistics, including the Z-test, F-test, G-test, and Pearson's chi-squared test, are tests for nested models and can be phrased as log-likelihood ratios or approximations thereof.
In the simple-vs-simple case, the likelihood ratio Λ(x) = L(θ0 | x) / L(θ1 | x) is small when the alternative model is better than the null model.
In the normal-population example with unknown mean and standard deviation, the likelihood ratio is λ = (1 + t²/(n−1))^(−n/2), where t is the t-statistic with n−1 degrees of freedom.
The example is adapted and abridged from Stuart, Ord & Arnold (1999, §22.2).
The article cites Neyman and Pearson (1933) for the problem of the most efficient tests of statistical hypotheses, published in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A.
